glossary.definition: An umbrella term encapsulating Augmented Reality (AR), Virtual Reality (VR), and Mixed Reality (MR).
Technology that overlays digital information or holograms onto the real world.
A completely immersive digital environment that replaces the user's real-world surroundings.
A blend of physical and digital worlds where real and holographic objects co-exist and interact in real-time.
Human-machine interaction in which the machine retains and manipulates referents to real objects and spaces (e.g., Apple Vision Pro).
A collective virtual shared space, created by the convergence of virtually enhanced physical reality and physically persistent virtual space.
A feature in VR/MR headsets that uses exterior cameras to show the user the real world inside the headset.
Passthrough video rendered in full color, crucial for high-quality Mixed Reality experiences.
Wearable computer glasses that add information alongside or to what the wearer sees.
A display device worn on the head or as part of a helmet.
A headset that contains all necessary processing power and batteries internally, requiring no external PC or console.
A headset that requires a physical cable connection to a PC, console, or smartphone to function.
A thin piece of glass or plastic that channels projected light directly into the user's eye using internal reflection. Common in AR glasses.
A type of waveguide that uses slanted nano-gratings to bend and direct light into the eye (e.g., HoloLens, Magic Leap).
Also known as geometric waveguides, these use an array of microscopic partially-reflective mirrors to direct light (e.g., Lumus).
A waveguide that uses holographic optical elements (HOEs) created by laser interference patterns to guide light.
An optical design where light from a microdisplay is bounced off a beam splitter to a curved mirror, which reflects it into the eye. Bulky but provides excellent image quality (e.g., XREAL).
Folded optics that bounce light back and forth between optical layers to drastically reduce the distance between the display and the lens, making headsets thinner.
A lens divided into a set of concentric annular sections. Used in older VR headsets to reduce weight and thickness, but often suffers from 'god rays'.
Lenses with surface profiles that are not portions of a sphere. They provide a clearer image with a larger sweet spot than Fresnel lenses.
Complex, non-symmetrical lens shapes designed to correct optical aberrations in highly compact AR/VR designs.
An optical device that splits a beam of light in two, used in AR to combine the display image with the real world.
The optical element in an AR headset where the virtual image is combined with the user's view of the real world.
An optical component that uses a hologram to alter the path of light, often acting as a lens, mirror, or combiner.
A property of light in an optical system, characterizing how 'spread out' the light is in area and angle. Crucial for AR optical efficiency.
The optical property of a material having a refractive index that depends on the polarization and propagation direction of light. Important in Pancake lenses.
Color fringing caused by a lens failing to focus all colors to the same convergence point. Software often corrects this in VR.
An optical effect where the image bends inward toward the center. VR software intentionally applies barrel distortion to counter this.
An optical effect where the image bulges outward. Applied in software to counteract the pincushion distortion of VR lenses.
Glare or light streaks visible in high-contrast scenes, heavily associated with the ridges on Fresnel lenses.
The precise center area of a lens where the image is sharpest and clearest.
The 3D volume of space in which the user's pupil can be placed to see the entire display clearly without image cutoff.
The required distance from the outer surface of the lens to the user's eye to achieve the full viewing angle.
OLED displays built on a silicon wafer (OLEDoS). Extremely small, high pixel density, and deep blacks. Currently the gold standard for compact VR/AR.
Displays made of microscopic inorganic LEDs. Known for extreme brightness (millions of nits), long lifespan, and high contrast. Crucial for outdoor AR.
A reflective display technology using liquid crystals over a silicon backplane. Very bright, historically used in Magic Leap and HoloLens.
A display technology using millions of microscopic mirrors on a DMD chip. Excellent color and brightness, used in some AR projectors.
Standard display tech utilizing a backlight. Evolved into 'Fast-Switching LCD' for VR to reduce motion blur.
Active Matrix OLED. Used in early VR (like original Oculus Quest) for great colors and blacks, but suffers from screen door effect due to lower pixel density.
A display method that creates an image by rapidly sweeping a laser beam across the retina or a combiner (e.g., North Focals).
Directly projecting light into the eye to form an image on the retina, bypassing standard screens entirely.
A unit of measurement for luminance (brightness). AR glasses need thousands or millions of nits at the display level to combat sunlight.
A visual artifact where the fine lines between pixels become visible, resembling looking through a screen door. Highly mitigated by Micro-OLED.
Clouding or inconsistent brightness/color across a display, commonly seen in OLED panels at low brightness levels.
The arrangement of red, green, and blue sub-pixels. RGB stripe is preferred for text clarity over PenTile matrix.
Turning off the backlight in specific areas of an LCD screen to achieve deeper blacks. Used in high-end LCD headsets.
A lighting model in rendering that adds more realistic lighting to 3D scenes by simulating how light bounces off surfaces.
Tracking rotational movement only (pitch, yaw, roll). You can look around, but leaning or walking is not tracked.
Tracking both rotation and translation (pitch, yaw, roll + x, y, z axes). Allows you to walk around and lean into virtual objects.
The computational problem of constructing a map of an unknown environment while simultaneously keeping track of an agent's location within it.
Tracking where cameras/sensors are located on the headset itself, reading the environment to determine spatial position (e.g., Meta Quest).
Tracking where external cameras/sensors (like base stations) are placed in the room to track the headset and controllers (e.g., Valve Index).
An electronic device containing accelerometers, gyroscopes, and sometimes magnetometers. The baseline sensor for 3DoF tracking.
Light Detection and Ranging. A sensor that uses lasers to accurately measure depth and create 3D meshes of a room (found in Apple Vision Pro/iPad Pro).
A sensor that measures the time it takes for a light pulse to bounce back from an object to calculate depth.
Using internal IR cameras to track where the user's pupils are looking. Crucial for foveated rendering and intuitive UI interaction.
Using external cameras to track the joints and movements of the user's bare hands, replacing physical controllers.
Tracking a user's facial expressions (mouth, cheeks, brows) to map them onto a digital avatar in real-time.
Using extra sensors (trackers) placed on the hips, feet, and elbows to accurately track the entire human body in VR.
Technology that simulates the sense of touch using vibrations or force feedback in controllers or vests.
Invisible reference points placed in the real world by a headset's SLAM system, allowing virtual objects to persist in the same physical location over time.
Combining data from multiple sensors (e.g., camera + IMU) to improve tracking accuracy and reduce latency.
The process of estimating a device's position and orientation by combining visual data from cameras with inertial data from an IMU.
The extent of the observable world seen at any given moment. Human vision is roughly 200° horizontal; standard VR is ~100°; AR glasses are often 20°-50°.
A measurement of angular resolution. 60 PPD represents human retinal resolution. VR headsets typically range from 20 to 40 PPD.
The distance between the centers of the pupils of the eyes. Crucial for optical alignment in headsets to prevent eye strain.
How many times per second the display updates, measured in Hertz (Hz). Higher refresh rates (90Hz+) reduce motion sickness.
The time it takes for a user's physical movement to be reflected on the display. Must be under 20ms to avoid nausea.
The ratio of width to height of an image or screen. Varies widely in AR/VR based on optical design.
The simulated physical distance at which the virtual image appears to the eye. Most VR headsets have a fixed focal distance of 1.5 to 2 meters.
A rendering technique that uses eye-tracking to render the area you are looking at in high resolution, while blurring the periphery to save massive processing power.
Rendering the center of the lenses in high resolution and the edges in low resolution, without eye tracking.
Techniques that artificially generate intermediate frames based on head movement when a game drops below the target framerate (e.g., Asynchronous Spacewarp/ASW).
Software algorithm that warps RGB channels inversely to the physical lens distortion to ensure colors align properly in the eye.
Eye strain caused when the eyes cross (vergence) to look at a close virtual object, but focus (accommodation) at the fixed distance of the screen. Solved by varifocal displays.
A display system that physically or optically shifts the focal plane to match where the user's eyes are converging, fixing VAC.
A display that projects multiple light rays from every point, allowing the eye to naturally focus at different depths. The ultimate theoretical solution to VAC.
The ability of a system to understand depth so that real-world objects can visually block (occlude) virtual objects, and vice versa.
An open standard API developed by the Khronos Group, allowing developers to write VR/AR apps that work across multiple headset brands.
An API for web browsers allowing them to run AR and VR experiences directly on a web page without app installations.
Video captured using multiple cameras to create a 3D hologram of a person or scene that can be viewed from any angle.
A novel rendering technique that creates highly photorealistic 3D scenes from 2D photos by representing them as 3D Gaussians instead of polygons.
An AI technique that generates novel views of complex 3D scenes based on a partial set of 2D images.
The science of making measurements from photographs, specifically used to generate 3D models from overlapping 2D images.
3D audio processing that makes sounds appear to come from specific locations in 3D space, matching virtual objects.
An algorithm used in spatial audio to simulate how sound interacts with the human head and ears to create accurate 3D sound positioning.
Audio technology that transmits sound vibrations directly through the skull to the inner ear, bypassing the eardrum. Often used in minimalist smart glasses.
Directional speakers built into the temples of smart glasses that project sound to the ears without blocking external ambient noise.
A wearable input device worn on the finger, increasingly used to discretely control AR glasses via micro-gestures.
A wearable band (usually on the wrist) that reads electrical signals from muscles to detect finger and hand movements before they physically happen (e.g., Meta's neural wristband).
A system that directly connects the human nervous system or brain to a computer, such as non-invasive wristbands or invasive chips (BCI).
AR headsets and software designed for industrial use, such as remote assistance, 3D CAD visualization, or medical training (e.g., HoloLens 2).
AR glasses meant for everyday use by the general public, prioritizing style, weight, and price over complex features.
A set of technologies which allow a person to feel as if they were present, to give the appearance of being present, or to have an effect, via telerobotics, at a place other than their true location.
A highly accurate virtual replica of a physical object, system, or environment, updated in real-time. Heavily used in enterprise XR.
A distortion artifact where the image warps or shifts unnaturally as the user moves their eye (pupil) around the lens.
A common VR locomotion method where the user points to a spot and instantly teleports there, eliminating motion sickness.
Moving in VR using a thumbstick, similar to traditional FPS games. Highly immersive but can cause nausea in sensitive users.
Rotating the virtual camera in rigid increments (e.g., 45 degrees) rather than smoothly, to reduce motion sickness.
A technique used in VR software to dynamically darken the edges of the screen during fast movement, reducing peripheral motion sickness.
Installing apps on a standalone headset from outside its official app store (e.g., using SideQuest).
An Oculus (Meta) technique that warps the last rendered frame to match the user's latest head movement, preventing jitter when frames drop.
Foveated rendering that actively tracks the pupil in real-time, shifting the high-resolution area exactly where the eye looks.
The distance between the optical centers of the left and right lenses in a headset. Must be adjustable to match user IPD.
A technique for creating or enhancing the illusion of depth in an image by means of stereopsis for binocular vision.
The inward turning of the eyes to focus on near objects. Crucial for depth perception in AR/VR.
Software calibration applied at the factory to offset the uneven brightness of individual pixels in OLED panels.
An optical phenomenon where light traveling through a medium hits a boundary and reflects entirely back into the medium. The core principle of waveguides.
A 3D image formed by the interference of light beams from a laser or other coherent light source.
The miniaturized projector inside AR glasses (often micro-OLED or Micro-LED) that shines light into the waveguide.
The measurement of Field of View from corner to corner. Often used in marketing to produce a larger number than horizontal FOV.
The measurement of Field of View from side to side. The most critical metric for immersion.
Recording a subject from all angles simultaneously to create a fully 3D, animated asset.
A digital representation of the user in a virtual space. Can be realistic or highly stylized.
Inverse Kinematics. A software calculation used to guess the position of elbows and knees based only on the position of the headset and controllers.
Google's augmented reality development platform for Android devices.
Apple's augmented reality development framework for iOS devices.
Apple's high-level 3D framework tailored specifically for AR and spatial computing.
A VR experience designed to allow the user to freely walk around a designated physical space.
A VR experience designed to be played while sitting in a chair, often relying on thumbsticks for movement.
A protective grid or cage in VR that appears when the user steps out of a small, fixed area, usually used for sitting or standing without walking.
The virtual boundary system (named by Meta and Valve, respectively) that prevents users from walking into physical walls.
The frequency at which the display updates the image. 72Hz is considered the bare minimum for VR, with 90Hz to 120Hz being preferred.
Stray light reflecting internally within the lens assembly, washing out contrast. Common in Pancake optics if anti-reflective coatings aren't perfect.
A visual artifact where a faint duplicate of an image appears, often caused by slow pixel response times or optical reflections.
An artifact specific to OLED displays in VR, where pixels take too long to turn back on after being completely black, causing a dark blur during head movement.
The total latency from physical movement, to sensor reading, to rendering, to the display updating. High MTP causes nausea.
The specific distance at which the eye must focus to see the virtual image clearly. Multi-focal displays use multiple planes to simulate depth.
